Chapter One: How Segregation Became the American Neighborhood
When you look at the neighborhoods around you—who lives where, which streets feel inviting, and which ones don’t—it’s tempting to think that all of this just sort of happened. Maybe it’s about who could afford a certain place, or who wanted to live nearby. But the truth? The way American neighborhoods look today comes from choices made in city halls, federal agencies, and local planning boards.
Those dividing lines between communities? They weren’t drawn by chance, or by some invisible force of the market. They were drawn on purpose, block by block, by people in power.
Imagine a family in the 1940s, full of hope, searching for the right place to settle after the war. They flip through the newspaper, picturing a little yard where their kids can play. But as they walk through new developments, the doors are closed, and the answers are always polite, but firm. Why? Because they’re Black—and the neighborhoods they visit have been designed to shut them out. There might not always be a sign, but the message is loud and clear: these homes aren’t for you.
Most of us grow up thinking that segregation in housing just happened because of personal preference, or maybe because of money. We hear that people “just ended up” living apart, that it all came down to private choices. That story gets told so often, it almost feels like common sense. But here’s something to pay attention to: the real story is much more unsettling.
The separation of Black and white families into different neighborhoods wasn’t just something the government allowed—it was something they enforced.
All over the country, local officials passed laws that made it illegal for Black families to move into white neighborhoods. And when the courts struck those laws down, city leaders got creative. They rewrote zoning rules, reserving some areas for single-family homes only. That might sound harmless, but it made sure that anyone who couldn’t afford those homes—usually Black families—were kept out. Even when the law didn’t mention race, the intent was crystal clear.
Federal agencies helped, too. The very programs meant to help families buy homes were set up to exclude Black Americans. Take the Federal Housing Administration. It refused to insure mortgages in neighborhoods where Black families lived, or even might move in. This practice, called “redlining,” stamped entire parts of cities as too risky for investment, just because of the people who lived there.
For families hoping to build a better life, these weren’t just hurdles—they were brick walls. Picture a Black parent working two jobs, saving every penny, only to find the doors to homeownership still locked. Meanwhile, white families with similar incomes were invited into new neighborhoods with loans backed by the government and affordable down payments. Over time, these differences didn’t just stay the same—they grew, shaping not only where people lived, but what kind of opportunities their children would have.
So, the story of American segregation isn’t just about an address. It’s about who gets the chance to build wealth, who can send their kids to good schools, and who feels safe walking their own street. The lines drawn on old maps still echo in families’ lives today. And if we want to change that story, the first step is to really understand how it got written in the first place.
